record.paper_title: Geodesic Nets: Some Examples and Open Problems
record.original_question: Let Sigma be the subset of (R^2)^3 consisting of triples S = (p1, p2, p3) for which, for every integer N, there exists a finite connected geodesic multinet in the Euclidean plane whose unbalanced vertices are exactly p1, p2, p3, whose edges are straight-line segments carrying positive integer multiplicities and may intersect or self-intersect, whose balanced vertices satisfy the multiplicity-weighted zero-sum tangent condition, and whose number of balanced vertices is at least N. Must Sigma have Lebesgue measure zero in (R^2)^3?

evidence.quote: In this case above definition says that a geodesic multinet is a graph G = (V, E) in Rn such that 1) S is a subset of the set of vertices V , 2) each edge is a straight line segment between its endpoints, and is endowed with a positive integer multiplicity

Problem 3.1.3. Let Σ be the set of all triples S of points of the Euclidean plane such that there exist geodesic multinets with 3 unbalanced vertices at S and arbitrarily many balanced vertices. Is it true that Σ is a set of measure zero (in (R2)3)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. A finite geodesic multinet is a finite connected graph $G=(V,E)$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (edges allowed to cross or self-intersect) such that:
(i) each edge $e \in E$ is a straight line segment between its two endpoints and is assigned a positive integer multiplicity $m(e) \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$;
(ii) the vertex set $V$ is partitioned into "balanced" and "unbalanced" vertices; at every balanced vertex $v$, the weighted sum of outgoing unit tangent vectors vanishes, i.e. $\sum_{e \ni v} m(e)\, \mathbf{u}_{v,e} = 0$, where $\mathbf{u}_{v,e}$ is the unit vector at $v$ pointing along the edge $e$.

Let $\Sigma \subset (\mathbb{R}^2)^3$ denote the set of ordered triples $S=(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that for every integer $N \geq 1$ there exists a finite connected geodesic multinet whose set of unbalanced vertices is exactly $\{p_1,p_2,p_3\}$ and which has at least $N$ balanced vertices.

Question: Does $\Sigma$ have Lebesgue measure zero in $(\mathbb{R}^2)^3 \cong \mathbb{R}^6$?
artifact.status_search_result: Recent works on geodesic nets with few boundary (unbalanced) vertices continue to investigate this question and related ones, but no source found resolves whether the set Σ has Lebesgue measure zero. The question is listed as an open problem in surveys on geodesic nets, and subsequent papers (e.g., on three- and four-boundary-vertex geodesic nets, 2024–2025) address related constructions without settling the measure-zero question.

status_evidence.title: Geodesic Nets: Some Examples and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Collection of open problems about geodesic nets, including questions about geodesic multinets with three unbalanced vertices.
status_evidence.claim: Problem is posed as an open question.

status_evidence.title: On the existence of a balanced vertex in geodesic nets with three boundary vertices
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2024) work on geodesic nets with three boundary/unbalanced vertices, treating related existence and structure problems.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent research addresses related three-boundary-vertex problems but does not resolve the measure-zero question.

status_evidence.title: Towards Constructing Geodesic Nets with Four Boundary Vertices and an Increasing Number of Balanced Vertices
status_evidence.snippet: 2025 paper constructing geodesic nets with many balanced vertices for four boundary points; the three-boundary-vertex measure-zero question is not settled here.
status_evidence.claim: Active research area; the specific measure-zero question remains unresolved in cited literature.
